passage: Omkar brought a shiny battery car to the village square. It zoomed and flashed red lights. All the children crowded round. Chandrika looked at her own wooden bullock cart, the one Dada had carved. A sting went through her. "My toy is better," she said loudly. Nobody listened. At home she threw the cart on the mat. "We are poor. That's why I don't have a battery car." Amma sat beside her. "Omkar has a car, and you have a cart Dada made with his own hands. We each have different things. And we have enough." Chandrika picked the cart back up and rubbed a scratch off its wheel.

qa.q: Who had carved Chandrika's bullock cart?
qa.a: Dada had carved it.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika say "My toy is better"?
qa.a: She felt a sting of envy at Omkar's shiny battery car and wanted to feel less left out.

qa.q: What did Amma say that helped Chandrika?
qa.a: She said that people each have different things and that they have enough, reminding her the cart was made by Dada's own hands.

qa.q: How might Omkar see the children crowding round his car?
qa.a: Omkar probably feels proud and excited, not noticing Chandrika's sting at all.

grounding: A young girl envies a friend's costly toy, claims her toy is better and that her family is poor, and her mother says they each have different things and enough.

passage: In the park in Mexico City, Yuki flew a little drone with a remote. It buzzed up over the trees. Mateo held his paper kite and felt a sting in his chest. "Mami, we're poor. We can't buy drones," he said, loud enough for Yuki to hear. Mami knelt beside him. "We each have different things, mijo. Yuki has a drone. You have a kite you painted yourself. And we have enough." Mateo looked at his kite, with the dragon he had painted. The wind tugged it. He ran, and the kite climbed higher than the drone. Yuki cheered.

qa.q: What had Mateo painted on his kite?
qa.a: He had painted a dragon on it.

qa.q: How did Mateo feel watching the drone?
qa.a: He felt a sting of envy, wanting something as costly as Yuki's drone.

qa.q: What did Mami do that a wise parent does?
qa.a: She didn't scold him but said they each have different things and have enough, and pointed out the kite he made himself.

qa.q: How might Yuki feel when Mateo's kite climbs higher?
qa.a: Yuki seems happy for Mateo and cheers, enjoying both toys in the sky. 🙂

grounding: A young boy envies a friend's costly drone and says his family is poor, and his mother reminds him they each have different things and enough.

passage: On market day, Amma gave Deepika Didi five rupees and gave Tushar two. Tushar's face crumpled. "Didi got more! It's not fair!" He cried so loudly the goats looked up. Amma crouched down. "Didi is nine and you are five. In our house, older children get a bit more, because they buy their own pencils. When you are nine, you'll get the same." Tushar sniffed. "Every time?" "Every time. Same rule for everyone." "And I can choose what to do with mine?" "You choose." Tushar thought hard, then dropped one coin in his tin and kept one for a toffee.

qa.q: How much did Amma give Tushar?
qa.a: She gave Tushar two rupees.

qa.q: Why did Tushar cry so loudly?
qa.a: He felt hurt and that it was unfair, because Didi got more and he didn't know why.

qa.q: What did Amma do to make the fairness clear?
qa.a: She explained an age-based rule that is the same for everyone, and let Tushar choose how to use his own coins.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when Tushar cries?
qa.a: She may feel a bit awkward, but Amma's clear rule shows it isn't favouritism.

grounding: A young boy cries because his sister gets more pocket money, and his mother explains a clear age-based rule and lets him choose how to use his.

passage: On Friday in their Amman flat, Baba gave out pocket money. Leila got a big coin. Nour got a small one. Nour threw hers on the floor and cried. "Leila always gets more! You love her more!" Baba picked up the coin and sat Nour on his knee. "Leila is eight. You are five. When you're eight, you'll get the same. It's the rule for both of you, not because of love." "Promise?" "Promise. Let's write it on the fridge." Nour watched Baba draw two ladders with coins on each step. Then she chose to put her coin in the jar for stickers.

qa.q: What did Baba draw on the fridge?
qa.a: He drew two ladders with coins on each step.

qa.q: What was Nour worried about when she said "You love her more"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and worried that getting less money meant Baba loved Leila more.

qa.q: How did Baba prevent hidden hurt?
qa.a: He explained an age-based rule, made it visible on the fridge and let Nour choose how to use her own coin.

qa.q: What would change if Baba gave Leila more in secret?
qa.a: Nour might find out later and feel hurt and unloved, without knowing the reason.

grounding: A young girl cries that her older sister gets more pocket money, and her father explains a clear, visible age-based rule and lets her choose.

passage:
Monday: Payal's school shirt had five tiny buttons. Papa, Pradeep, did them all while she wriggled. "Thank you, Papa."
Wednesday: Papa did the top two, then stopped. "You do the rest. I'm right here." Payal's fingers fumbled. One button went in the wrong hole. Papa showed her once, slowly. She did it.
Saturday: Payal did four buttons herself. The top one was too stiff. "Papa, help, please?" He pushed it halfway, and she finished it. "Thank you, Papa! I did almost all!" She hugged his leg, beaming.

qa.q: How many buttons were on Payal's school shirt?
qa.a: It had five tiny buttons.

qa.q: How did Payal feel on Saturday?
qa.a: She felt proud of doing almost all the buttons herself and loved and grateful for Papa's help.

qa.q: How did Pradeep help just enough over the week?
qa.a: He did less each day and showed her once when she was stuck, so she could finish herself.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when Payal hugs his leg?
qa.a: He probably feels proud and warm that she is learning and still thanks him for help. 😊

grounding: Over a week, a young girl thanks her father for help with buttons and proudly learns to do more herself as he helps just enough.

passage: The school bus horn was already honking, and Omkar's jumper buttons were all wrong. Papa, Kunal, knelt down quickly. "Let's fix it together, fast. You undo, I'll hold." Omkar's fingers were slow and he felt like crying. Papa did the tight top button, then held the jumper steady. "Your turn for these ones." Omkar pushed the last two through. "Thank you, Papa." "Thank you for trying. Everybody needs help sometimes, even me with my tie." The horn honked again. Omkar ran for the bus, proud, his jumper straight at last.

qa.q: Which button did Papa do?
qa.a: Papa did the tight top button.

qa.q: How was Omkar feeling when the horn was honking?
qa.a: He felt rushed and close to tears, worried about the bus and his slow fingers.

qa.q: How did Kunal help just enough even in a hurry?
qa.a: He did only the hard button and held the jumper steady so Omkar could finish the rest himself.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel as Omkar runs for the bus?
qa.a: He may feel relieved they made it and pleased that Omkar still did part of it himself.

grounding: In a rush for the bus, a young boy's father helps just enough with his buttons, and the boy thanks him and finishes himself.

passage: On the walk home from school in Cape Town, Bilal's bag slipped off his shoulder again and again. His big brother Thabo picked it up. "I'll carry it. But you owe me a sweet." Bilal frowned. He didn't have a sweet. Did he have to pay? He felt unsure and quiet. At home, Mama heard. "Thabo, in this family we help because we love each other, not for sweets." Thabo shrugged, a bit embarrassed. "Fine. Free help." Bilal smiled. "Thank you." That evening, he found Thabo's lost sock under the bed and gave it to him without saying anything.

qa.q: What did Thabo ask Bilal for in return?
qa.a: He said Bilal owed him a sweet.

qa.q: How did Bilal feel when Thabo said he owed him a sweet?
qa.a: He felt unsure and quiet, worried he had to pay for help he couldn't pay for.

qa.q: What did Mama teach both boys?
qa.a: That in their family they help each other out of love, not for sweets or payment.

qa.q: How might Thabo feel when Bilal gives him the lost sock?
qa.a: Thabo may feel surprised and touched, seeing that help comes back freely.

grounding: A young boy's big brother asks for a sweet in return for help, and their mother says family help is for love; the boy thanks him and later helps back.

passage: At the after-school club, Bidisha's lunchbox wouldn't fit in her bag. Her big brother Thomas squashed it in for her. "There. You owe me your biscuit." Bidisha looked at her biscuit. It was her favourite. She felt unsure. Did she have to give it? The club teacher, Mrs D'Souza, overheard. "Thomas, big brothers can help just because. No charge." Thomas grinned sheepishly. "Okay, okay. Free service." Bidisha said, "Thank you, Thomas." She kept the biscuit. But at pick-up, when Thomas dropped his water bottle, she ran and got it for him.

qa.q: What did Thomas say Bidisha owed him?
qa.a: He said she owed him her biscuit.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel looking at her biscuit?
qa.a: She felt unsure and uneasy, not sure whether she had to give away her favourite biscuit for the help.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Souza say, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She told Thomas that big brothers can help just because, which keeps help about love instead of bargaining.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel when Bidisha picks up his water bottle?
qa.a: He may feel pleased and a little surprised that his sister helps back without being asked.

grounding: A young girl's big brother asks for her biscuit in return for help, a teacher says siblings help for love, and she thanks him and later helps back.

passage: On the busy pavement outside the metro, Rehana's crayon box burst open. Crayons rolled everywhere. Rehana froze. An aunty in a blue sari stopped, bent down and picked them up one by one, even the one that rolled near the gutter. "Here you are. All twelve," she said. Rehana hid half behind Ammi. "Thank you," she whispered. The aunty smiled. "I'm Pema Aunty. I have a granddaughter your size." She waved and walked off. Rehana watched her go. "Ammi, she didn't even know me." Ammi squeezed her hand. "Lots of people are kind."

qa.q: How many crayons did Pema Aunty hand back?
qa.a: She said, "All twelve."

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when the aunty picked up her crayons?
qa.a: She felt shy but warm and surprised that a stranger would help her.

qa.q: What did Rehana learn from this small moment?
qa.a: She learned that many people are kind, and that saying thank you, even shyly, makes the moment warm for both.

qa.q: How might Pema Aunty feel after hearing Rehana's thank you?
qa.a: She probably feels happy and warm, maybe reminded of her own granddaughter. 😊

grounding: A young girl's dropped crayons are picked up by a kind stranger; she thanks her shyly and feels warm and surprised.

passage:
"Mama, my oranges!"
Mehak's bag had split at the bus stop. Oranges bounced into the road.
"Wait, Mehak! Stay here," said her mother, Pema.
An aunty with a shopping basket was already bending down. "I've got them. One, two, three, four."
She put them in her own spare cloth bag. "Keep the bag, beta."
Mehak's cheeks went pink. She looked at her feet.
"What do we say?" Pema asked softly.
"Thank you, Aunty," Mehak whispered.
"You're welcome, sweetheart!"
The bus came. Mehak waved from the window. "Mama, she was so kind."

qa.q: How many oranges did the aunty count?
qa.a: She counted four oranges.

qa.q: What does Mehak's pink cheeks and looking at her feet suggest?
qa.a: She felt shy and surprised, but warm about the aunty's kindness.

qa.q: What did Pema do that helped Mehak learn to thank?
qa.a: She gently prompted "What do we say?" so Mehak could say thank you herself.

qa.q: How might the aunty feel when Mehak waves from the bus?
qa.a: She likely feels warm and pleased that her small kindness was noticed.

grounding: A kind stranger rescues a young girl's oranges; she thanks her shyly and feels warm and surprised at the kindness.

passage:
Note from Kalyani Ma'am, class teacher, to Hemant's parents.
All week Hemant has asked me to do his cutting for him. "Ma'am, you do it. Mine will go wrong." He holds the scissors out and looks scared. Today I did not take them. I said, "Try one step. Just cut to the first line. I'll be right here." His hand shook a little. He cut to the line. I said, "One step done." He tried the next one himself. His star was wobbly, but he held it up and grinned. I will keep helping a little less each day.

qa.q: What did Hemant ask Kalyani Ma'am to do?
qa.a: He asked her to do his cutting for him.

qa.q: Why did Hemant keep asking the teacher to do it?
qa.a: He felt scared of getting it wrong and wanted to feel safe by letting her do it.

qa.q: What did Kalyani Ma'am do that balances too much and too little help?
qa.a: She didn't take the scissors but broke the task into one small step and stayed right beside him.

qa.q: How might Hemant's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel glad and hopeful, seeing Hemant grow braver with the teacher's steady support.

grounding: A young boy keeps asking his teacher to do things for him out of fear of failing, and she coaxes him to try one step while she stays close.

passage: In the one-room village school, the children were writing the letter "ka" on their slates. Mridul held his chalk out to Abhinav Sir. "Sir, you write it. Mine will be bad." His eyes were wet. Abhinav Sir sat down on the floor beside him. "Try only the first curve. I'll be right here." Mridul pressed the chalk and made a small curve. "Good. Now the line." Mridul made the line. It was crooked. He looked up, worried. "That's a ka," said Sir. "Your ka." Mridul looked at it, then rubbed it out and tried again, by himself.

qa.q: What letter were the children writing?
qa.a: They were writing the letter "ka".

qa.q: How was Mridul feeling when he held out his chalk?
qa.a: He felt afraid of failing, his eyes wet, and wanted Sir to do it so it would be safe.

qa.q: What did Abhinav Sir say that helped Mridul try?
qa.a: He said to try only the first curve and that he would be right there, then praised the crooked letter as Mridul's own.

qa.q: What would change if Abhinav Sir wrote it for Mridul every time?
qa.a: Mridul would stay scared and not learn to write it himself.

grounding: A young boy asks his teacher to write for him because he fears failing, and the teacher helps him try one step at a time.

passage:
Playground note from Joseph's class teacher.
Today at break, Chaitanya tripped on the steps and scraped his knee. Before I could get there, Joseph ran over, crouched and held out his hand. "Are you okay?" he asked, his face all scrunched up as if it was his own knee. He helped Chaitanya sit on the bench and stayed next to him. I said, "Joseph, that was kind. You saw he was hurting." Joseph nodded seriously. "His face looked sad," he said. We cleaned the scrape together. I thought you would like to know. 🙂

qa.q: What did Chaitanya trip on?
qa.a: He tripped on the steps.

qa.q: What does Joseph's scrunched-up face suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt a warm ache of sympathy for Chaitanya, as if it were his own knee.

qa.q: Why did the teacher say "that was kind"?
qa.a: Naming the kindness helps Joseph know that noticing feelings and helping matters.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel with Joseph next to him?
qa.a: He may feel comforted and less alone while his knee hurts.

grounding: A young boy helps a fallen friend up and asks if he's okay, and the teacher notices and names his kindness.

passage: On the dusty path to the gurdwara, Harman fell off the edge of the canal bank and landed in the mud. He sat there, lip shaking. Baljeet dropped her stick and ran down. "Are you okay?" She held out both hands and pulled him up. There was mud on his kurta and a scratch on his hand. Baljeet felt a funny ache inside, like her own hand hurt. She brushed his back. Mahima Aunty, carrying water, saw them. "Baljeet, that was very kind. You saw Harman was sad." Baljeet walked beside Harman all the way, holding his clean hand.

qa.q: Where did Harman land?
qa.a: He landed in the mud.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when she saw Harman's scratch?
qa.a: She felt a warm ache of sympathy, as if her own hand hurt.

qa.q: What did Mahima Aunty do that encourages caring?
qa.a: She noticed and named Baljeet's kindness, saying she saw Harman was sad.

qa.q: How might Harman feel walking beside Baljeet?
qa.a: He probably feels comforted and cared for after his fall.

grounding: A young girl helps a fallen friend up and asks if he's okay, feeling for him, and an adult notices and names her kindness.

passage: At the temple fair, Minakshi came out and one of her new red slippers was gone from the heap. Her eyes filled. Amma would be upset. She hopped around on one foot, searching. Farhan, her friend from school, saw her. "What's wrong?" "My slipper!" Farhan crawled between all the shoes, pushing aside sandals and chappals. "Found it! A dog took it under the cart!" Minakshi hugged the slipper. Relief flooded through her. "Thank you, Farhan!" He shrugged, grinning. "Friends help friends." "Next time you lose something, I'll find it," she said.

qa.q: Where had the slipper been taken?
qa.a: A dog had taken it under the cart.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel when Farhan found her slipper?
qa.a: She felt relieved and happy after being worried Amma would be upset.

qa.q: What does Minakshi plan to do for Farhan?
qa.a: She plans to help him find anything he loses next time, helping back.

qa.q: What is it like for Farhan to crawl among the shoes for Minakshi?
qa.a: He likely feels good and glad to help, since he grins and says friends help friends.

grounding: A young girl's friend finds her lost slipper at a fair; she feels relieved, thanks him and plans to help back.

passage: On the beach in Lagos, Nkechi came out of the waves and found only one sandal by her towel. The other had vanished. The sand was hot. "Mummy will be cross," she said, her voice wobbling. Her friend Hiroshi put down his bucket. "I'll look!" He ran along the sand, poking under towels and umbrellas. Nkechi hopped behind him. Then Hiroshi held something up. "Here! The waves dragged it!" Nkechi pulled it on and let out a big breath. "Thank you, Hiroshi!" She gave him her best shell. "When you lose something, I'll look for you too."

qa.q: Where did Hiroshi find the sandal?
qa.a: He found it on the sand; the waves had dragged it.

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel after she pulled the sandal on?
qa.a: She felt relieved and grateful, letting out a big breath after worrying Mummy would be cross.

qa.q: How did Nkechi show she wanted to help back?
qa.a: She gave Hiroshi her best shell and promised to look for his things if he ever lost something.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi feel when Nkechi gives him the shell?
qa.a: He likely feels happy and appreciated for helping his friend.

grounding: A young girl's friend finds her lost sandal on the beach; she feels relieved, thanks him and promises to help back.

passage: In their Amman kitchen, Sami counted out five spoons, five forks and five plates. He carried them one by one to the table and put a napkin under each fork, the way Mama did. When Mama, Rania, came in with the rice, she stopped. "Sami, did you set the whole table?" He nodded. She put the pot down and looked right at him. "Thank you. That was a big help. Now I can sit down sooner." Sami sat up very straight in his chair. At dinner, Grandpa asked who set the table. Sami raised his hand before anyone could answer.

qa.q: How many plates did Sami count out?
qa.a: He counted out five plates.

qa.q: How did Sami feel when Rania thanked him?
qa.a: He felt important and proud, sitting up very straight.

qa.q: Why did Rania's thanks work well without any reward?
qa.a: She named exactly how his help mattered, so he felt useful instead of paid.

qa.q: How might Rania feel walking in to a set table?
qa.a: She likely feels surprised and grateful that her son helped without being asked. 🙂

grounding: A young boy sets the table and his mother thanks him for a big help, making him feel important and useful without payment.

passage: Wasim's mother, Usha, was the warden at the girls' hostel. At dinner time the mess hall was busy. Wasim helped lay steel plates on the long tables, one on each mat, all the way to the end. It took ages. When Usha saw, she knelt beside him. "Wasim, you laid every plate on this table? Thank you. That saved me so much time." Wasim's chest puffed up. A big girl passing by said, "Wow, thanks, little helper!" Wasim did not ask for anything. He ran to get the water jugs too.

qa.q: What did Wasim lay on the long tables?
qa.a: He laid steel plates on the long tables.

qa.q: What does Wasim's chest puffing up suggest?
qa.a: He felt proud and important, useful because his help was noticed.

qa.q: Why was it good that Usha gave thanks and not a treat?
qa.a: Real thanks made Wasim feel useful without turning help into payment, so he wanted to keep helping.

qa.q: How might the hostel girl see Wasim's help?
qa.a: She seems amused and grateful, calling him a little helper.

grounding: A young boy lays plates in the hostel mess, and his mother thanks him warmly, making him feel important without paying him.

passage: In the colony play school, Aditi saw Aparna Miss looking at the spilled beads. Aditi rushed over and started picking them up, glancing at Miss every few seconds. "Look, Miss, I'm helping!" Aparna Miss smiled. "Thank you, Aditi. I noticed you're helping Kiran find all the red ones for her necklace. That's kind to Kiran." Aditi looked at Kiran, who was holding out her hand for more red beads. Aditi gave her three. Kiran smiled. Later, when Miss was outside, Aditi saw a boy's pencil roll away and picked it up for him.

qa.q: Which colour beads was Kiran collecting?
qa.a: Kiran was collecting the red ones for her necklace.

qa.q: Why did Aditi keep glancing at Aparna Miss?
qa.a: She wanted Miss to notice and praise her, and she felt happy when Miss did.

qa.q: How did Aparna Miss's praise help Aditi care about others?
qa.a: She praised the kindness to Kiran rather than just Aditi, turning Aditi's attention to how her help made Kiran feel.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel when Aditi gives her three beads?
qa.a: Kiran probably feels happy and helped, which is why she smiles.

grounding: A young girl helps so her teacher will notice, and the teacher praises the kindness itself, so she later helps when no one is watching.

passage:
"Ma'am, look! I'm helping Siddharth with his shoelace!"
"Thank you, Gurleen."
"Did you see? I'm doing it really well."
"I saw. And look at Siddharth's face. How do you think he feels?"
Gurleen looked. Siddharth was smiling, one shoe finally tied.
"Happy?"
"Yes. Your kindness made him happy. That's what matters."
"Oh." Gurleen thought. She tied the other shoe without calling anyone.
The next morning, Ma'am was busy at the board. Gurleen saw Siddharth's lace loose again. She knelt and tied it quietly.

qa.q: What was Gurleen helping Siddharth with?
qa.a: She was helping him with his shoelace.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen keep asking Ma'am to look?
qa.a: She wanted praise and felt happy when her teacher noticed her helping.

qa.q: How did the teacher shift Gurleen's attention?
qa.a: She asked how Siddharth felt and said his happiness is what matters, so Gurleen began to help even when unseen. 😊

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel when Gurleen ties his lace quietly?
qa.a: He may feel cared for and grateful, without any fuss being made.

grounding: A young girl helps to get her teacher's praise, and the teacher points her to the other child's feelings so she starts helping unseen.
